name: journal-pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh.json
content:
What was Paul's thorn in the flesh? Nobody knows, and Paul never says. He writes that "a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me",1 and he leaves it there. Readers have guessed at it for nineteen centuries. The guesses tell us less about the thorn than the passage around it tells us about the man who wrote it.

What Paul wrote

In 2 Corinthians 12 Paul is boasting, and he says he does it under protest. He will go on, he writes, "to visions and revelations of the Lord".2 He knows "a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows".3 The man "heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter".4

The man is Paul. He speaks of himself in the third person, and he gives a date only as "fourteen years ago" without saying which year or which place. No other person saw the event, and nothing that was said can be repeated. A claim that arrives with no witness and no content is a claim that only the claimant can confirm.

[paulus_figure name="rays-of-light-through-clouds-40340600"]Rays of light through cloud. Paul says he was "caught up to the third heaven" and heard "things that cannot be told" (2 Corinthians 12:2–4).[/paulus_figure]

Then comes the thorn. It was given, he says, "to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations".5 He prayed: "Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me."6 The answer he reports was private as well: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness."7

The guesses

Church writers have proposed headaches, earache, eye trouble, malaria, epilepsy, a speech difficulty and a struggle with desire. Some read the thorn as people: the opponents who followed Paul from church to church. The text allows several of these and proves none.

The eyes get the most support from Paul's other letters. He reminds the Galatians that "it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first",8 and that they would have "gouged out your eyes and given them to me".9 He ends the letter in his own hand: "See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand."10 That fits poor sight. It fits other things as well, and [paulus_link slug="ego-epilepsy-and-narcissism" /] weighs the case for epilepsy against what the letters actually describe.

Why he wrote it

The reason matters more than the diagnosis. The Corinthians had met rivals who boasted of visions and of their own standing, and some of them had said that Paul's "bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account".11 Chapter 12 is his reply. He answers a charge of weakness by producing a revelation that no one can test, and then turns the weakness itself into proof of divine favour.

The move works on a reader who already trusts him. It does nothing for a reader who asks how anyone would know. [paulus_link slug="the-damascus-road" /] shows the same pattern at Damascus, where the one claim of seeing the Lord rests on Paul's word, and [paulus_link slug="revelation-or-borrowing" /] asks how much of what he calls revelation he could have received from men.

[paulus_figure name="thorn-branch-thorns-37176612"]A thorn branch. Paul calls his affliction "a thorn in the flesh" and never names it (2 Corinthians 12:7).[/paulus_figure]

A habit of revelations

The thorn passage is no isolated claim. When Paul needs authority, a private revelation arrives. He says his gospel came "through a revelation of Jesus Christ".12 He went up to Jerusalem "because of a revelation" and set his gospel before the leaders "privately".13 He lists his own sight of the risen Christ last in the line of witnesses, "as to one untimely born".14

Each time the evidence is Paul's word, in a setting where no one else was present. The third heaven is the same kind of claim, made louder because the Corinthians were doubting him.

A Muslim reading

A messenger of God receives a revelation to deliver to his people, and the people can examine it, repeat it and hold it against what came before. A revelation that "cannot be told" cannot be examined at all. Paul placed the centre of his authority in something he says he must not repeat. That is a poor foundation for a teaching that millions were asked to take as the word of God.

The verdict

Paul's afflictions are in his letters and can be believed. His visions are in his letters too, and they come with no witness and no content. He says he heard things that cannot be repeated, then used them to defend his authority against people who doubted him.

A private revelation that no one can examine proves nothing except that its author wanted to be believed. [paulus_link slug="lord-before-the-spirit" /] sets out what a teaching built on such claims takes the place of.

Paul's thorn in the flesh: questions readers ask

What was Paul's thorn in the flesh?

Paul does not say. He calls it "a messenger of Satan to harass me" (2 Corinthians 12:7). Proposals include eye trouble, headaches, epilepsy, a speech problem and human opponents, and none can be shown from the text.

Did Paul have bad eyesight?

Possibly. Galatians 4:15 speaks of eyes and 6:11 of "large letters", but neither verse says that his sight was poor.

What was the third heaven?

Paul uses the phrase once, of a man "caught up to the third heaven" fourteen years before he wrote (2 Corinthians 12:2). He does not describe it.

Did anyone else see Paul's visions?

No source reports a witness. In 2 Corinthians 12 Paul is the only person who tells of the vision and the answer to his prayer.
